report.summary: Anthropic is reportedly building a new kind of source control, betting that AI agents like Claude writing code at scale will break Git-era version control.
report.background: Version control has been shaped by Git since 2005, when Linus Torvalds built it for a kernel project written by humans at human pace. Commits were meaningful units of intent, branches were expensive, and review was a social process. AI coding assistants upended those assumptions: Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code and autonomous agents now generate code far faster than people can read it. Agents commit constantly, spin up speculative branches in parallel, and create or resolve merge conflicts at machine speed, while the humans nominally in charge increasingly approve diffs they have not truly read. Anthropic, whose Claude models are among the most widely used for coding, is reportedly rethinking source control itself rather than bolting agents onto Git. The move fits a broader 2026 pattern: vendors are rebuilding developer infrastructure around the assumption that the primary author of code is a model, not a person.
key_points: Git's core assumptions no longer hold. It was designed for infrequent, human-authored, human-reviewed commits. Agents produce thousands of tiny changes, parallel speculative branches, and merge churn at a volume that makes commit history, blame, and linear branching models nearly meaningless as a description of what actually happened.

An agent-native system would likely shift the unit of change from a diff to an intent. Expect commits tied to a task or prompt, provenance metadata naming the model and agent run, cheap snapshot-style branching, machine-readable conflict resolution, and policy gates that run before code ever reaches a human.

Review, not authoring, is now the bottleneck. Since reviewers cannot read generated code at the rate it appears, trust has to come from automated verification: tests, static analysis, formal checks, and auditable provenance trails that satisfy compliance and security teams.

The real prize is owning the system of record for agent work. GitHub, GitLab, Google and a wave of startups are all racing to be where agents push code, because whoever holds that position controls workflows, permissions, and distribution for the next decade of development.

Lock-in and trust are the obvious risks. A proprietary source-control layer tuned to one vendor's models raises portability and governance questions, and Anthropic's own safety incidents during testing show why enterprises will demand auditability before ceding their repositories.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a land-grab moment: source control is sticky infrastructure, and whoever makes it agent-native gains enormous leverage over how models are used. For developers, expect less manual diff review and more work designing verification, policy, and intent specifications, with Git fluency remaining valuable but no longer sufficient. Smaller teams may ship far more software, while large enterprises gain machine-checkable audit trails for regulated code. For regular users, the practical effect is faster, cheaper software and more frequent updates, plus a harder question: when nobody fully reads the code, who is accountable when it fails? Provenance and automated testing become the substitute for human review.
report.tools: Watch Jujutsu (jj), Meta's Sapling, Graphite and GitButler, which already experiment with stacked and agent-friendly workflows. For verification, look at CodeRabbit, GitHub's Copilot code review, and SLSA/sigstore for provenance signing. For running agents safely, sandboxing platforms like E2B and Daytona matter, alongside Claude Code and Cursor. Any emerging Anthropic source-control offering should be evaluated against these for portability and audit support.
